o: We must build a new string where each character `s[i]` lands at position `indices[i]`. This is a pure permutation problem: since all values in `indices` are unique and valid, the mapping is a bijection, so every output slot is filled exactly once. For Example 1, `s[0]='c'` goes to index 4, `s[4]='l'` goes to index 0, etc., producing "leetcode". For Example 2, `indices = [0,1,2]` is the identity permutation, so nothing changes. With $n \le 100$, any $O(n)$ or even $O(n^2)$ approach works; the natural optimal solution is a single pass filling a result buffer.
k: The mapping is a bijection: every character has a unique destination, so one pass of direct placement fills the answer completely.
Building a result array and writing `res[indices[i]] = s[i]` avoids any need for sorting or in-place cycle chasing.
Strings are immutable in Python/Java/JS, so use a char array (or list) and join at the end.

a.n: Approach 1: Direct Placement with Auxiliary Buffer
a.i: Create an array of size n. For each i, place s[i] at position indices[i]. Because indices is a permutation of 0..n-1, every slot gets written exactly once, so no collisions occur and the result is correct after one pass.
s: Allocate a result array/list of length n.
Join/convert res back into a string and return it.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the input plus O(n) to build the result string.
a.sp: O(n) — auxiliary buffer for the shuffled characters (required since strings are immutable in most languages).

a.n: Approach 2: In-Place Cyclic Permutation (O(1) extra space)
a.i: If we may modify `s`, we can follow cycles: repeatedly swap s[i] into its target slot indices[i], then update indices[i] to remember where that displaced character still needs to go. Each swap places at least one character permanently, giving O(n) total swaps without extra storage.
s: Convert s to a mutable char array.
For each i from 0 to n-1: while indices[i] != i, swap chars[i] with chars[indices[i]] and swap indices[i] with indices[indices[i]].
Return the char array as a string.
a.t: O(n) — each swap fixes at least one element in its final position, so total swaps across all cycles are at most n.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the mutable copies needed because strings are immutable in Python/Java/JS (truly O(1) only in languages like C++ where s can be modified directly).

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1 — it's simple, obviously correct, and optimal at O(n). Mention Approach 2 as a follow-up if asked to do it in-place with O(1) space. Common pitfalls: forgetting that strings are immutable (need char arrays), misreading the direction of the mapping (it's res[indices[i]] = s[i], not res[i] = s[indices[i]] — both actually work here since indices is a permutation, but be consistent), and assuming duplicates could exist in indices (the constraints guarantee uniqueness). Edge cases: n = 1 and identity permutations. Likely follow-ups: solve in-place, handle when indices contains invalid values, or generalize to shuffling by a k-step rotation.
